cells.tense: Fairness moves through you as a felt sense, and you are not working at it.
cells.ask: Change one arrangement that has quietly tilted toward someone else, and say out loud that you changed it — once, plainly, as yours.
cells.core:
You can feel when a thing has tilted — a favor run too long one way, a room where the give stopped going both directions — and you adjust it without a spreadsheet in your head. What you decide lands. You say this, not that, and the people around you feel the rightness of it even when they can't say why. That steadiness is doing real work in your life right now, mostly below the surface, mostly unremarked.

And balance is a practice, not a place you arrive at once. An ending sits next to this — something that has finished its run and is being carried past its usefulness. The fair thing and the finished thing are often the same thing. Keep the feel. Let what's over be over, and let the next arrangement be a real one.
cells.sheetLine: You feel the tilt and you adjust it. That's already working.
cells.verb: calibrating what's out of proportion and easing it back toward fair

cells.tense: You are building a ledger of who owes what in advance of any harm, bracing against a bill nobody has sent yet.
cells.ask: Pick one tally you've been keeping this week — a debt, a slight, an expected thank-you — and set it down unfilled for a day. If the day ends without it hurting, leave it.
cells.core:
The sense of what's fair is still running. It's just running ahead of events now, tracking debts before anyone has spoken them. You notice who took more than their share, who hasn't returned the call, what you're owed and by when. The counting feels like care, and under the counting is something you'd rather hold at arm's length: the fear that if you stop watching the scale, you'll be tilted against and not notice.

No one likes being managed by a ledger, including you. The body doesn't keep accounts well — it just gets tired. And the thing you're braced for hasn't happened. Where you can let a debt stay open for a while and hold the discomfort without settling it, you're giving yourself back the steady equal ground the tally was taken to protect.
cells.sheetLine: You're collecting on a debt nobody has actually charged you.

cells.tense: You stopped asking for what is owed a long time ago, and you are still standing there having stopped.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you need, small enough to be ordinary — not a demand, a statement. Then let it sit without adding a reason.
cells.core:
You have a clear enough eye for what's fair; that isn't what's missing. What's missing is the move toward it — the asking, the claim, the saying-so. Wanting your due went somewhere you don't want to return to, and the want itself got quiet. Now you take what comes and call it fine. You don't quite believe that word, but it's easier than the other one.

Your own sense of proportion is real and it hasn't gone anywhere. The bit that's out of practice is the small, steady act of standing behind it. Practicing in tiny ordinary places builds the strength without setting off the alarm. You won't have everything owed you today. Today is for one small truth said plainly, and for noticing that the world did not tilt off its axis when you said it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped asking for what's yours and made peace with it.

cells.tense: You are keeping score of old complaints without knowing you are keeping score, and the tally is already written.
cells.ask: When you next notice a complaint rising, name to yourself what you're actually owed. If nothing in the moment is owed, say so plainly and put the tally down.
cells.core:
The scale is already running. It's weighing slights, favors, what so-and-so said, what you gave and didn't get. You didn't decide to start the tally, and you'd probably say you're not a scorekeeper. That's the misattribution — the running operates without your say-so, and it steers more of your next move than you'd guess.

There's a simpler knowing available than the ledger version. It's quiet, it doesn't argue, and it tends to be right about what actually matters. The counting says it's just keeping things accurate — but accurate about what? If the scale is running, it's fair to notice what it's for. If it isn't serving anything you'd choose, you can stop picking it up. That's not naivety. That's you deciding. One of the tallies you're carrying could belong to a simpler read instead.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping accounts you didn't choose to open.
